BEGIN READER ARTICLE

# What Is Malolactic Fermentation?

## Highlights

- Malolactic fermentation (MLF) is a bacterial conversion that changes malic acid into lactic acid and carbon dioxide.
- It is different from alcoholic fermentation, which is driven mainly by yeast and produces alcohol.
- MLF can make acidity seem less sharp and may give wine a rounder texture.
- It can sometimes contribute buttery or creamy aromas, but it does not automatically make wine buttery.
- MLF is common in many red wines and is used selectively in white wines, including Australian Chardonnay.
- Winemakers may encourage, prevent or partly manage MLF depending on the style they want.

## Quick answer

Malolactic fermentation is a stage of winemaking in which lactic-acid bacteria convert malic acid into lactic acid and carbon dioxide.

Malic acid is a naturally occurring grape acid. It can contribute to a sharper, more angular impression in wine. Lactic acid is generally perceived as softer, so MLF usually reduces the sense of sharpness and changes the wine’s acid balance. It does not remove all acidity, and it does not guarantee that a wine will taste soft or creamy.

Despite its name, MLF is not the same as the alcoholic fermentation that produces wine’s alcohol. Alcoholic fermentation is mainly performed by yeast, which converts grape sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide. MLF is a bacterial conversion of acid.

Winemakers may allow MLF to happen naturally, use selected bacteria to manage it, prevent it, or allow it in only part of a wine. The decision depends on the grape, vintage, acidity, intended style and the wine’s need for stability.

## How does malolactic fermentation work?

During MLF, lactic-acid bacteria convert malic acid into lactic acid and carbon dioxide. One important wine-associated bacterium is *Oenococcus oeni*, although other lactic-acid bacteria can also be involved.

The two main biological processes look like this:

| Process | Main microorganism | Main change |
|---|---|---|
| Alcoholic fermentation | Yeast | Sugar becomes alcohol and carbon dioxide |
| Malolactic fermentation | Lactic-acid bacteria | Malic acid becomes lactic acid and carbon dioxide |

MLF often occurs after alcoholic fermentation, although winemakers can manage the timing in different ways. The important point for wine drinkers is that MLF is not simply “a second alcoholic fermentation”. It is more precisely a bacterial conversion, even though the traditional name remains malolactic fermentation.

## What does MLF do to wine?

### It can make acidity seem less sharp

MLF generally lowers a wine’s titratable acidity and raises its pH. In practical tasting terms, the wine may seem less sharp, angular or pointed.

That does not mean MLF makes a wine flat. A wine can still have plenty of refreshing acidity after MLF. Its final impression also depends on grape ripeness, alcohol, tannin, residual sugar, pH and the balance of other components.

This is why “softer” is best understood as a tasting description, not a guarantee. A soft-tasting wine has not necessarily undergone MLF.

### It may change texture

Some wines that have undergone MLF seem rounder or smoother on the palate. The altered acid balance can make the wine feel less tense, while other winemaking choices may contribute to a fuller or creamier impression.

MLF is only one possible influence on texture. Lees contact, oak, alcohol, blending and grape composition can also affect how a wine feels. These processes may be used alongside MLF, but they are not the same thing.

### It can sometimes add buttery or creamy aromas

MLF can contribute to the formation of diacetyl, a compound associated with buttery, creamy, nutty or dairy-like aromas. This is one reason people often connect MLF with buttery Chardonnay.

But MLF does not automatically make a wine taste like butter. The amount of diacetyl formed and retained varies with the bacteria, the wine and how it is handled. Some wines complete MLF with little obvious buttery aroma.

A creamy or buttery impression may also come from oak, lees contact or a combination of influences. Aroma alone is therefore not a reliable test for whether MLF occurred.

## Why do winemakers use MLF?

MLF is a choice, not a compulsory stage in every wine.

A winemaker may encourage it to:

- reduce a wine’s sharper acid impression;
- shape the wine’s texture;
- develop a particular style;
- contribute certain aroma characteristics; or
- reduce the chance of an unwanted bacterial conversion happening later in the bottle.

A winemaker may prevent or limit it to:

- preserve bright, energetic freshness;
- retain more of the original malic-acid character;
- protect a delicate aromatic style;
- avoid excessive softening; or
- avoid prominent buttery or dairy-like aromas.

Sometimes only part of a wine undergoes MLF. This can help a winemaker balance freshness with texture before blending.

Completing MLF may also support biological stability by reducing the amount of malic acid available for a later, unwanted bacterial conversion. However, it is not a complete guarantee of bottle stability; many aspects of wine chemistry and packaging contribute to that.

## Does every wine undergo malolactic fermentation?

No. MLF is common in many red wines, but it is not universal. It is also used in some white wines, while others undergo only partial MLF or none at all.

For Australian wine drinkers, MLF is especially relevant because it is encountered frequently in Australian red wine and selectively in Australian white wine. A historical Australian Wine Research Institute survey estimated that MLF was used in approximately 99% of Australian red table wine and 11% of Australian white table wine in its surveyed dataset. Those figures are historical survey results, not current universal statistics.

Australian Chardonnay is a useful example of winemaking choice. It may be made with full, partial or no MLF. A wine with MLF may seem rounder or creamier, while one that avoids it may retain a sharper, more linear acid profile. Oak, lees contact, ripeness and other decisions also influence the result.

Australian practice is not uniform. Choices vary by grape variety, vintage, winery, fruit acidity and intended style.

## MLF, oak and lees: what is the difference?

These terms are easy to mix up:

- **MLF** is a bacterial conversion of malic acid into lactic acid.
- **Oak maturation** means wine has contact with oak, which can contribute characters such as vanilla, spice or toast.
- **Lees contact** means wine is kept with the spent yeast cells left after fermentation, which can influence texture and savoury or creamy impressions.

A winemaker may use two or all three techniques in the same wine. A buttery or creamy wine does not therefore point to one process by itself.

For broader context, see [how wine is made](/how-wine-is-made/), [what Chardonnay is](/what-is-chardonnay/) and [what oak does to wine](/winemaking/oak.html).

## Is malolactic fermentation good or bad?

Neither. MLF is a winemaking tool, and whether it is useful depends on the wine being made.

In a high-acid wine, reducing some sharpness may help create a more balanced style. In another wine, preserving that sharpness may be the goal. A winemaker may want buttery complexity in one Chardonnay but a bright, clean and linear style in another.

The question is not whether MLF is inherently good. It is whether the conversion suits the wine’s intended balance, texture, aroma and stability.

## Can you taste whether a wine has undergone MLF?

Not reliably from one sensation alone.

A wine that has undergone MLF may seem less sharply acidic, rounder or more textured, and it may show buttery or creamy aromas. But those impressions can also result from alcohol, oak, lees, fruit ripeness, blending and other production choices.

The most useful approach is to treat MLF as one possible explanation rather than a tasting diagnosis. If a wine tastes soft, that does not prove MLF occurred. If it tastes buttery, that does not prove oak was used—or that MLF was the only cause.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is malolactic fermentation the same as fermentation?

It is commonly called a fermentation, but technically it is a bacterial conversion or decarboxylation. It is different from yeast-driven alcoholic fermentation.

### Does MLF make wine less acidic?

It generally reduces titratable acidity and raises pH, so acidity may seem less sharp. It does not remove all acidity or guarantee a flat wine.

### Is buttery Chardonnay always made with MLF?

No. MLF can contribute to buttery aromas through diacetyl, but oak, lees contact and other factors may also contribute. MLF does not always produce a buttery character.

### Does MLF happen in red wine or white wine?

It is common in many red wines and is selective in white wines. Australian Chardonnay may undergo full, partial or no MLF.

### Can MLF happen naturally?

Yes. It can occur through bacteria already present in the winery or wine, or it can be managed using selected bacterial cultures.

**Job ID;** WD-0502

**Topic;** What is malolactic fermentation?

**Primary question;** What is malolactic fermentation, how does it change wine, and why do winemakers use it?

**Decision;** Approve for Research handover.

**Priority and rationale;** P1 because this is a foundational wine-science concept with direct relevance to acidity, texture, aroma and winemaking decisions. It extends the deployed fermentation page into a useful explanatory child page and helps readers interpret styles such as fuller, softer or creamy wines without turning the article into product promotion.

**Article type;** Educational Guide — target 1,000–1,800 words, written to usefulness rather than an arbitrary word count.

**Research depth;** 2 Standard. The article needs reliable technical explanation, terminology control, sensory implications, safety/contextual accuracy and Australian examples, but not a historical or specialist canonical treatment.

**Page type;** Foundational explanatory article / cluster child.

**Primary entity;** Malolactic fermentation (MLF), the biologically mediated conversion of malic acid to lactic acid in wine.

**Parent cluster;** Winemaking and wine science, with primary parent `WD-0501 — What is fermentation?`

**Audience and intent;** Australian beginners and curious intermediate wine drinkers seeking a clear definition and practical understanding. Intent is primarily informational: definition, process, effect on taste and whether it occurs in all wines.

**Highlights the reader should leave with;**

- MLF is not the same process as the alcoholic fermentation that produces alcohol.
- It is a conversion of sharper malic acid into softer lactic acid, carried out by lactic-acid bacteria.
- It can reduce perceived sharpness and alter texture and aroma, but it does not simply make every wine “better”.
- Winemakers may encourage, prevent, or partially manage it depending on the desired wine style and stability.
- MLF is common in many red wines and selected white wines, including some Chardonnays, but it is not universal.
- “Malolactic fermentation” is technically a decarboxylation process and should not be presented as yeast fermentation.

**Scope;**

1. Give a plain-English definition near the beginning.
2. Distinguish alcoholic fermentation from MLF.
3. Explain malic acid, lactic acid and the role of lactic-acid bacteria at an appropriate level.
4. Describe broad sensory and structural effects: acidity perception, mouthfeel and possible buttery or dairy-associated aroma compounds.
5. Explain why a winemaker may encourage, block, or manage MLF.
6. Cover red wine and white wine applications without implying a universal rule.
7. Explain the relationship between MLF, lees, oak and maturation only where necessary and accurately.
8. Include practical answers to whether MLF is good, whether it happens in all wine, and whether drinkers can identify it.
9. Use Australian examples carefully, especially Chardonnay and cool-climate or regional style variation, without claiming that Australian wine follows one national practice.
10. Link conceptually to fermentation, acidity, wine body, tasting and relevant grape/style pages where appropriate.

**Exclusions;**

- Do not draft a winemaking recipe or provide cellar- or winery-operational instructions.
- Do not give unsafe advice about inducing bacterial fermentation at home.
- Do not claim MLF is caused by yeast, is identical to alcoholic fermentation, or always produces a buttery flavour.
- Do not present “softness” as proof that MLF occurred.
- Do not make unsupported claims about particular Australian producers, regions or brands.
- Do not duplicate a separate future article on acidity, Chardonnay, wine body or yeast; explain only what is needed for this question.
- Do not use pilot article copy or pilot research outputs.

**Required Australian context;**

- Explain that MLF is relevant to Australian wine consumers because it is encountered in common Australian styles, especially many red wines and some Australian Chardonnays.
- Avoid treating Australian practice as uniform; note that choices vary by grape, vintage, winery and intended style.
- Use Australian spelling and terminology.
- Research should verify any Australian-specific examples or claims before publication.

## Direct Factual Answer

**Malolactic fermentation is a bacterial conversion in wine in which lactic-acid bacteria transform malic acid into lactic acid and carbon dioxide.** The process generally reduces titratable acidity and increases pH, which can make a wine seem less sharply acidic. It may also alter mouthfeel and aroma, including sometimes contributing buttery or dairy-associated notes through the formation of diacetyl. ([oiv.int](https://www.oiv.int/standards/international-code-of-oenological-practices/part-ii-oenological-treatments-and-practices/wines/microbiological-de-acidification-by-lactic-acid-bacteria))

Despite its name, MLF is not the same as alcoholic fermentation. Alcoholic fermentation is primarily performed by yeast, which converts sugar into alcohol and carbon dioxide. MLF is performed by lactic-acid bacteria and usually occurs after, or partly alongside, alcoholic fermentation. ([oiv.int](https://www.oiv.int/standards/international-code-of-oenological-practices/part-ii-oenological-treatments-and-practices/wines/microbiological-de-acidification-by-lactic-acid-bacteria))

MLF is not compulsory and does not automatically improve a wine. Winemakers may encourage it, prevent it, or allow it to occur in only part of a wine depending on grape variety, acidity, desired style, stability and cellar conditions.

## Key Claims and Evidence

### 1. MLF converts malic acid into lactic acid

**Sourced fact:** Lactic-acid bacteria used in oenology transform malic acid into lactic acid and carbon dioxide. The OIV identifies this conversion as microbiological de-acidification. ([oiv.int](https://www.oiv.int/de/standards/international-oenological-codex/part-i-monographs/monographs/lactic-acid-bacteria?utm_source=openai))

**Recommended Editorial wording:**

> During malolactic fermentation, naturally occurring or selected lactic-acid bacteria convert sharper-tasting malic acid into softer lactic acid.

The word “softer” is useful for beginners but should be treated as a sensory description rather than a complete chemical definition. Lactic acid is generally perceived as less sharp than malic acid, but the finished wine’s acidity also depends on pH, total acidity, grape composition, alcohol and other compounds.

**Technical note:** MLF is more precisely a decarboxylation or bacterial conversion than a fermentation in the same sense as alcoholic fermentation. Editorial can explain this briefly without overloading the article with biochemistry.

---

### 2. MLF is performed by lactic-acid bacteria, not yeast

The most important organism associated with wine MLF is **Oenococcus oeni**, although the OIV’s oenological codex recognises relevant lactic-acid bacteria from several genera, including *Oenococcus*, *Leuconostoc*, *Lactobacillus* and *Pediococcus*. ([oiv.int](https://www.oiv.int/de/standards/international-oenological-codex/part-i-monographs/monographs/lactic-acid-bacteria?utm_source=openai))

The article should distinguish the two main biological processes:

| Process | Main microorganism | Main substrate | Main products |
|---|---|---|---|
| Alcoholic fermentation | Yeast | Sugars | Alcohol and carbon dioxide |
| Malolactic fermentation/conversion | Lactic-acid bacteria | Malic acid | Lactic acid and carbon dioxide |

This table or equivalent explanation would prevent the common misconception that MLF is simply a second yeast fermentation.

**Qualification:** MLF can occur spontaneously through bacteria already present in the winery or wine, or it can be initiated with selected bacterial cultures. ([oiv.int](https://www.oiv.int/standards/international-code-of-oenological-practices/part-ii-oenological-treatments-and-practices/wines/microbiological-de-acidification-by-lactic-acid-bacteria))

---

### 3. MLF changes acidity and pH

The OIV defines the process partly through its effect on acidity: MLF reduces titratable acidity and increases actual acidity pH. ([oiv.int](https://www.oiv.int/standards/international-code-of-oenological-practices/part-ii-oenological-treatments-and-practices/wines/microbiological-de-acidification-by-lactic-acid-bacteria))

For ordinary readers, the distinction should be explained carefully:

- **Titratable acidity** refers broadly to the total amount of acid that can be measured by neutralisation.
- **pH** describes the strength of acidity in the solution.
- These measures are related but are not identical.
- A change in both can affect how the wine tastes, but MLF does not remove all acidity.

Recommended consumer wording:

> MLF usually lowers the wine’s total acid load and raises its pH, so the wine may taste less sharp or angular. It does not make the wine acid-free.

The article should avoid saying that MLF “removes acidity” without qualification. It changes the acid profile; it does not eliminate acidity or guarantee a soft wine.

---

### 4. MLF can change mouthfeel

MLF may make a wine seem rounder, softer or less pointed because malic acid has been converted and the overall acid balance has changed. It may also contribute to a different perception of body or texture.

These sensory outcomes should remain qualified. “Softness” is not proof that MLF occurred, and MLF is only one contributor to mouthfeel. Other relevant influences include:

- grape ripeness;
- alcohol;
- residual sugar;
- tannin;
- lees contact;
- oak;
- blending;
- pH and total acidity;
- fermentation and maturation choices.

The article should not state that MLF always makes wine fuller-bodied or creamy. A safe formulation is:

> MLF can make acidity feel less sharp and may contribute to a rounder texture, but the effect depends on the wine and the other choices made during production.

This distinction is important because some wines undergo MLF without developing an obvious creamy character.

---

### 5. Diacetyl can produce buttery or dairy-associated aromas

Diacetyl is a compound associated with buttery, creamy, nutty or dairy-like aroma descriptions. Lactic-acid bacteria may produce diacetyl during or around MLF, but the amount formed and retained depends on bacterial strain, wine composition, timing and subsequent handling. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0168160504002867?utm_source=openai))

The article should explicitly prevent the common shortcut:

> MLF does not always make wine taste buttery.

A wine can undergo complete MLF and show little obvious butter character. Conversely, a buttery impression may be influenced by other factors, including oak, lees contact, fermentation compounds or the interaction of several aroma compounds.

Recommended wording:

> Some MLF wines show buttery or creamy aromas because the bacteria can produce diacetyl. But MLF is not synonymous with buttery Chardonnay, and the aroma is neither automatic nor universal.

Avoid presenting a single fixed “butter threshold” unless the article is prepared to explain that sensory thresholds vary by wine matrix and taster. The available specialist literature indicates that moderate diacetyl may contribute complexity, while higher concentrations can become dominant or undesirable, but these figures are unnecessary for the approved beginner article. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/topics/agricultural-and-biological-sciences/malolactic-fermentation?utm_source=openai))

---

### 6. MLF can contribute to microbiological stability

The OIV identifies biological stability as one objective of MLF. Completing the conversion can reduce the risk that residual malic acid is later consumed by bacteria in the bottle, which could otherwise cause unwanted changes such as gas formation, turbidity or flavour instability. ([oiv.int](https://www.oiv.int/standards/international-code-of-oenological-practices/part-ii-oenological-treatments-and-practices/wines/microbiological-de-acidification-by-lactic-acid-bacteria))

This point should be included briefly and without operational advice:

> Winemakers may also complete MLF before bottling to reduce the risk of an unwanted bacterial conversion occurring later in the bottle.

Editorial should not imply that MLF is the only route to wine stability or that every wine containing malic acid is unstable. The issue depends on wine chemistry, microbial population, sulphur dioxide management, filtration and other cellar controls.

---

### 7. MLF is optional and can be encouraged, prevented or managed

MLF is a winemaking choice rather than an automatic stage in every wine. It can occur:

- spontaneously through indigenous bacteria;
- through inoculation with selected bacterial cultures;
- after alcoholic fermentation;
- in some cases, earlier through co-inoculation or sequentially managed approaches.

AWRI describes traditional post-alcoholic-fermentation inoculation as common, while also documenting interest in earlier inoculation strategies. ([awri.com.au](https://www.awri.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2011/06/Malolactic-fermentation.pdf))

For a consumer article, the practical reasons can be summarised as:

**A winemaker may encourage MLF to:**

- reduce sharp acidity;
- alter mouthfeel;
- develop a particular style;
- contribute selected aroma characteristics;
- improve biological stability;
- manage the wine consistently.

**A winemaker may prevent or limit MLF to:**

- preserve bright, high-acid freshness;
- retain malic-acid character;
- protect a delicate aromatic style;
- avoid excessive softening;
- avoid unwanted buttery or dairy-associated aromas;
- reduce the risk of an uncontrolled conversion later.

**A winemaker may use partial MLF to:**

- blend wines with different acid profiles;
- retain some freshness while adding texture;
- balance style and stability objectives.

Avoid describing these as guaranteed outcomes. The decision varies by grape, vintage, pH, alcohol, winery practice and intended style.

---

### 8. MLF does not occur in all wines

MLF is common in red wine but not universal. It is also used in some white wines, particularly selected Chardonnay styles, but many white wines do not undergo full MLF.

An AWRI national winery-practices survey reported that approximately **99% of Australian red table wine** and **11% of Australian white table wine** underwent MLF in the survey dataset. These figures are historical survey results and should not be presented as current universal production statistics. They are useful evidence that MLF is widespread in Australian red wine and selective in white wine. ([awri.com.au](https://www.awri.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2019/05/AWRI_Practices_Survey_Final_Report.pdf))

Recommended wording:

> MLF is common in many red wines, while white wines are more likely to be made with full, partial or no MLF depending on the intended style.

Do not claim that every red wine undergoes MLF or that white wine never does.

---

### 9. Chardonnay is a relevant white-wine example

Wine Australia describes Chardonnay as an adaptable Australian variety made in a wide range of styles. Its current variety profile notes that Australian winemakers use full, partial or no MLF, and that attitudes toward the technique continue to evolve. ([wineaustralia.com](https://www.wineaustralia.com/market-insights/regions-and-varieties/chardonnay))

This supports a restrained Australian example:

> Australian Chardonnay may be made with full, partial or no MLF. A wine with full or partial MLF may seem rounder or creamier, while a wine that avoids MLF may retain a sharper, more linear acid profile—but the final result also depends on oak, lees contact, ripeness and other winemaking choices.

The article should not imply that all Australian Chardonnay is buttery, that cool-climate Chardonnay avoids MLF, or that MLF alone explains the style of a particular region.

---

### 10. MLF is separate from oak and lees ageing

The article needs a concise terminology distinction because consumers often associate buttery or creamy Chardonnay with several production choices.

- **MLF:** bacterial conversion of malic acid to lactic acid.
- **Oak maturation:** wine contact with oak, which may contribute compounds associated with vanilla, spice, toast or other characters.
- **Lees contact:** maturation on or with dead yeast cells, which may influence texture and savoury or creamy impressions.

These processes can occur together, but they are not interchangeable. A creamy or buttery wine may reflect MLF, oak, lees contact, or a combination. The presence of oak does not prove MLF, and MLF does not prove oak use.

This is a reasonable explanatory distinction based on the separate definitions of MLF and Wine Australia’s description of oak and lees as additional Chardonnay techniques. ([wineaustralia.com](https://www.wineaustralia.com/market-insights/regions-and-varieties/chardonnay))

## Definitions and Terminology Notes

### Malolactic fermentation

The biologically mediated conversion of malic acid into lactic acid and carbon dioxide by lactic-acid bacteria.

### Malolactic conversion

A technically more precise alternative because the process is not yeast fermentation. It is suitable for a short parenthetical note but should not replace the familiar term throughout the article.

### Malic acid

A naturally occurring grape acid often associated with a sharper, more angular or green-apple-like perception. Avoid presenting “green apple” as a universal tasting descriptor.

### Lactic acid

The acid produced when malic acid is converted during MLF. It is generally perceived as softer or less sharp than malic acid.

### Lactic-acid bacteria

The bacterial group responsible for MLF. *Oenococcus oeni* is the principal wine-associated organism to mention if Editorial wants one named example.

### Diacetyl

An aroma-active compound that may contribute buttery, creamy, nutty or dairy-associated notes. Its presence and sensory impact vary.

### Full MLF

Most or all available malic acid has been converted. This term should not be used to imply a fixed sensory result.

### Partial MLF

Only some of the wine or some of the malic acid has undergone conversion. It may be used to balance freshness and texture.

### Co-inoculation

MLF bacteria are introduced while alcoholic fermentation is still underway. This is a technical term that can be mentioned briefly but does not require procedural detail.

### Sequential inoculation

MLF bacteria are introduced after alcoholic fermentation. This is described by AWRI as the traditional and commonly used timing. ([awri.com.au](https://www.awri.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/MLF-in-white-and-sparkling-wine.pdf))

## Common Misconceptions to Prevent

1. **“MLF is the second alcoholic fermentation.”**  
   Incorrect. MLF is a bacterial conversion of malic acid.

2. **“MLF is caused by yeast.”**  
   Incorrect. Lactic-acid bacteria perform the conversion.

3. **“MLF removes all acidity.”**  
   Incorrect. It changes the acid profile and usually reduces perceived sharpness, but wine remains acidic.

4. **“Every wine undergoes MLF.”**  
   Incorrect. It is common in red wine and selective in white wine.

5. **“MLF always makes wine buttery.”**  
   Incorrect. Diacetyl may occur, but buttery aroma is not automatic.

6. **“Soft wine proves that MLF occurred.”**  
   Incorrect. Softness can result from many factors.

7. **“A buttery Chardonnay must have seen oak.”**  
   Incorrect. MLF, oak, lees contact or combinations may contribute.

8. **“MLF always improves wine.”**  
   Unsupported. It is a style and stability decision with benefits and trade-offs.

9. **“MLF and oak ageing are the same thing.”**  
   Incorrect.

10. **“Malolactic fermentation is always spontaneous.”**

## Conflicting or Uncertain Information

### Is MLF technically a fermentation?

The established industry term is “malolactic fermentation”, but technically the process is a bacterial decarboxylation or conversion rather than yeast fermentation. Editorial should retain the familiar term while explaining the distinction once.

### Does MLF always make wine softer?

The acid conversion commonly reduces sharpness, but perceived softness is influenced by total acidity, pH, alcohol, tannin, sugar, lees, oak and blending. Use “may make acidity seem softer” rather than “makes wine soft”.

### Does MLF always create diacetyl?

No. Diacetyl formation depends on bacterial strain and wine conditions, and the compound may subsequently be reduced or otherwise affect the final aroma differently. Do not treat buttery aroma as a diagnostic test for MLF. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0168160504002867?utm_source=openai))

### Is MLF always beneficial for stability?

Completing MLF can help reduce the risk of later bacterial conversion, but biological stability depends on multiple cellar and packaging factors. Avoid presenting MLF as a complete stability guarantee.

### Are Australian MLF percentages current?

The AWRI practices survey provides useful Australian evidence, but the published survey is historical and should not be presented as a current census. Use it to support broad context, not exact present-day market shares.

### Can a wine undergo MLF before alcoholic fermentation is complete?

Yes, co-inoculation and earlier inoculation strategies are documented, although sequential post-alcoholic-fermentation inoculation remains common. This need only be mentioned at a high level. ([awri.com.au](https://www.awri.com.au/wp-content/uploads/2018/03/MLF-in-white-and-sparkling-wine.pdf))

# What Is Malolactic Fermentation?

## Highlights

- Malolactic fermentation (MLF) is a bacterial conversion that changes malic acid into lactic acid and carbon dioxide.
- It is different from alcoholic fermentation, which is driven mainly by yeast and produces alcohol.
- MLF can make acidity seem less sharp and may give wine a rounder texture.
- It can sometimes contribute buttery or creamy aromas, but it does not automatically make wine buttery.
- MLF is common in many red wines and is used selectively in white wines, including Australian Chardonnay.
- Winemakers may encourage, prevent or partly manage MLF depending on the style they want.

## Quick answer

Malolactic fermentation is a stage of winemaking in which lactic-acid bacteria convert malic acid into lactic acid and carbon dioxide.

Malic acid is a naturally occurring grape acid. It can contribute to a sharper, more angular impression in wine. Lactic acid is generally perceived as softer, so MLF usually reduces the sense of sharpness and changes the wine’s acid balance. It does not remove all acidity, and it does not guarantee that a wine will taste soft or creamy.

Despite its name, MLF is not the same as the alcoholic fermentation that produces wine’s alcohol. Alcoholic fermentation is mainly performed by yeast, which converts grape sugars into alcohol and carbon dioxide. MLF is a bacterial conversion of acid.

Winemakers may allow MLF to happen naturally, use selected bacteria to manage it, prevent it, or allow it in only part of a wine. The decision depends on the grape, vintage, acidity, intended style and the wine’s need for stability.

## How does malolactic fermentation work?

During MLF, lactic-acid bacteria convert malic acid into lactic acid and carbon dioxide. One important wine-associated bacterium is *Oenococcus oeni*, although other lactic-acid bacteria can also be involved.

The two main biological processes look like this:

| Process | Main microorganism | Main change |
|---|---|---|
| Alcoholic fermentation | Yeast | Sugar becomes alcohol and carbon dioxide |
| Malolactic fermentation | Lactic-acid bacteria | Malic acid becomes lactic acid and carbon dioxide |

MLF often occurs after alcoholic fermentation, although winemakers can manage the timing in different ways. The important point for wine drinkers is that MLF is not simply “a second alcoholic fermentation”. It is more precisely a bacterial conversion, even though the traditional name remains malolactic fermentation.

## What does MLF do to wine?

### It can make acidity seem less sharp

MLF generally lowers a wine’s titratable acidity and raises its pH. In practical tasting terms, the wine may seem less sharp, angular or pointed.

That does not mean MLF makes a wine flat. A wine can still have plenty of refreshing acidity after MLF. Its final impression also depends on grape ripeness, alcohol, tannin, residual sugar, pH and the balance of other components.

This is why “softer” is best understood as a tasting description, not a guarantee. A soft-tasting wine has not necessarily undergone MLF.

### It may change texture

Some wines that have undergone MLF seem rounder or smoother on the palate. The altered acid balance can make the wine feel less tense, while other winemaking choices may contribute to a fuller or creamier impression.

MLF is only one possible influence on texture. Lees contact, oak, alcohol, blending and grape composition can also affect how a wine feels. These processes may be used alongside MLF, but they are not the same thing.

### It can sometimes add buttery or creamy aromas

MLF can contribute to the formation of diacetyl, a compound associated with buttery, creamy, nutty or dairy-like aromas. This is one reason people often connect MLF with buttery Chardonnay.

But MLF does not automatically make a wine taste like butter. The amount of diacetyl formed and retained varies with the bacteria, the wine and how it is handled. Some wines complete MLF with little obvious buttery aroma.

A creamy or buttery impression may also come from oak, lees contact or a combination of influences. Aroma alone is therefore not a reliable test for whether MLF occurred.

## Why do winemakers use MLF?

MLF is a choice, not a compulsory stage in every wine.

A winemaker may encourage it to:

- reduce a wine’s sharper acid impression;
- shape the wine’s texture;
- develop a particular style;
- contribute certain aroma characteristics; or
- reduce the chance of an unwanted bacterial conversion happening later in the bottle.

A winemaker may prevent or limit it to:

- preserve bright, energetic freshness;
- retain more of the original malic-acid character;
- protect a delicate aromatic style;
- avoid excessive softening; or
- avoid prominent buttery or dairy-like aromas.

Sometimes only part of a wine undergoes MLF. This can help a winemaker balance freshness with texture before blending.

Completing MLF may also support biological stability by reducing the amount of malic acid available for a later, unwanted bacterial conversion. However, it is not a complete guarantee of bottle stability; many aspects of wine chemistry and packaging contribute to that.

## Does every wine undergo malolactic fermentation?

No. MLF is common in many red wines, but it is not universal. It is also used in some white wines, while others undergo only partial MLF or none at all.

For Australian wine drinkers, MLF is especially relevant because it is encountered frequently in Australian red wine and selectively in Australian white wine. A historical Australian Wine Research Institute survey estimated that MLF was used in approximately 99% of Australian red table wine and 11% of Australian white table wine in its surveyed dataset. Those figures are historical survey results, not current universal statistics.

Australian Chardonnay is a useful example of winemaking choice. It may be made with full, partial or no MLF. A wine with MLF may seem rounder or creamier, while one that avoids it may retain a sharper, more linear acid profile. Oak, lees contact, ripeness and other decisions also influence the result.

Australian practice is not uniform. Choices vary by grape variety, vintage, winery, fruit acidity and intended style.

## MLF, oak and lees: what is the difference?

These terms are easy to mix up:

- **MLF** is a bacterial conversion of malic acid into lactic acid.
- **Oak maturation** means wine has contact with oak, which can contribute characters such as vanilla, spice or toast.
- **Lees contact** means wine is kept with the spent yeast cells left after fermentation, which can influence texture and savoury or creamy impressions.

A winemaker may use two or all three techniques in the same wine. A buttery or creamy wine does not therefore point to one process by itself.

For broader context, see [how wine is made](/how-wine-is-made/), [what Chardonnay is](/what-is-chardonnay/) and [what oak does to wine](/winemaking/oak.html).

## Is malolactic fermentation good or bad?

Neither. MLF is a winemaking tool, and whether it is useful depends on the wine being made.

In a high-acid wine, reducing some sharpness may help create a more balanced style. In another wine, preserving that sharpness may be the goal. A winemaker may want buttery complexity in one Chardonnay but a bright, clean and linear style in another.

The question is not whether MLF is inherently good. It is whether the conversion suits the wine’s intended balance, texture, aroma and stability.

## Can you taste whether a wine has undergone MLF?

Not reliably from one sensation alone.

A wine that has undergone MLF may seem less sharply acidic, rounder or more textured, and it may show buttery or creamy aromas. But those impressions can also result from alcohol, oak, lees, fruit ripeness, blending and other production choices.

The most useful approach is to treat MLF as one possible explanation rather than a tasting diagnosis. If a wine tastes soft, that does not prove MLF occurred. If it tastes buttery, that does not prove oak was used—or that MLF was the only cause.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is malolactic fermentation the same as fermentation?

It is commonly called a fermentation, but technically it is a bacterial conversion or decarboxylation. It is different from yeast-driven alcoholic fermentation.

### Does MLF make wine less acidic?

It generally reduces titratable acidity and raises pH, so acidity may seem less sharp. It does not remove all acidity or guarantee a flat wine.

### Is buttery Chardonnay always made with MLF?

No. MLF can contribute to buttery aromas through diacetyl, but oak, lees contact and other factors may also contribute. MLF does not always produce a buttery character.

### Does MLF happen in red wine or white wine?

It is common in many red wines and is selective in white wines. Australian Chardonnay may undergo full, partial or no MLF.

### Can MLF happen naturally?

Yes. It can occur through bacteria already present in the winery or wine, or it can be managed using selected bacterial cultures.
